For combination-unit long-haul trucks, FleetDNA data from rural freeways on weekdays (top left) match the bimodal distribution in MOVES3 but have a stronger presence in the earlier-hour peak than the later-hour one compared to MOVES3. For weekends (right-hand plots), FleetDNA also shows more time spent in earlier hours and less time in later hours compared to MOVES3; on other rural roads, the later peak has shrunk down to a shoulder off the earlier peak, and on urban freeways on weekends the distribution appears a bit bimodal, in contrast to the smooth singular peak in the MOVES3 distribution. For rural other roads and urban roads on weekdays, FleetDNA shows no bimodal trend, and more miles spent in earlier hours compared to MOVES3. Due to the large number of vehicles (around 70) and thousands of driving hours recorded, we recommend that MOVES3 consider updating their distribution to reflect these nuances in combination-unit long-haul VMT distributions. 73 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. Hour VMT fractions for FleetDNA combination-unit long-haul vehicles For combination-unit short-haul vehicles on urban roads on weekdays, FleetDNA does not display a bimodal trend like MOVES3 and instead drives more miles in the morning hours on freeways and midday hours on other roads, as shown in Figure 55 (bottom left two charts). Also, on urban other roads on weekends, FleetDNA trucks drive proportionally more in the morning and early afternoon, particularly from 5 a.m. to 2 p.m., and less in the evening compared to MOVES3. For weekdays, around 80 vehicles and hundreds of hours of data per hour ID compose these data. 74 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. Figure 55. Hour VMT fractions for FleetDNA combination-unit short-haul vehicles The FleetDNA data for single-unit short-haul vehicles contain more peaks in the VMT distribution than MOVES3. In particular, the FleetDNA VMT distribution has a peak around hour ID 11 on urban freeways on weekdays, in contrast to the MOVES3 smoother bimodal distribution. Per hour ID, urban freeways on weekdays contain around 30 vehicles and 30 hours on average, and urban other roads on weekdays 50 vehicles with hundreds of hours. The weekday urban other roads have a large peak in the late morning and a shoulder in the plot around evening rush hour, again contrasting the MOVES3 bimodal distribution. Compared to MOVES3, the FleetDNA single-unit short-haul vehicle data on weekend urban other roads have more driving hours in the early morning and less in the late evening, which is similar to the observations from the combination trucks shown in the previous plots. Despite the noise in the data, the FleetDNA data for urban other roads appear to be more characteristic of commercial vehicle behavior, compared to the bimodal MOVES3 trend, which is derived from both personal and commercial VMT. 75 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications.
